name: Amoebic Liver Abscess

possible: Concurrent or preceding intestinal amoebiasis (only a minority have concurrent diarrhea at presentation)
pathogens.why: Entamoeba histolytica is the specific cause of amoebic liver abscess, reaching the liver via the portal circulation after invading the colonic mucosa; the classic presentation is a single right-lobe abscess, which helps but does not definitively distinguish it from pyogenic abscess without aspirate/serology.

investigations.why: Characterizes the abscess (typically single, right lobe, in amoebic disease) and guides the decision on aspiration.
Highly sensitive for invasive amoebiasis and useful when aspiration is not performed or is inconclusive.
Supportive if positive, but a substantial proportion of liver abscess patients have negative stool studies at the time of presentation.

investigations.test: Diagnostic aspiration (if no improvement in 5-7 days, large/left-lobe abscess, or diagnostic uncertainty)
investigations.why: Classic 'anchovy paste' aspirate supports amoebic etiology; also allows bacterial culture to exclude/identify a pyogenic or mixed process.

reason: Right upper quadrant pain and fever without jaundice, in a patient from an endemic area (with or without a preceding diarrheal illness), raises suspicion for amoebic liver abscess — a classically single, right-lobe lesion caused by Entamoeba histolytica. This is distinguished from pyogenic liver abscess primarily by aspirate appearance/serology, but empiric metronidazole is appropriate to start given the high treatment success rate and relative safety, pending confirmation.

clinicalPearls: Most patients are febrile with right-upper-quadrant pain that may be dull or pleuritic and may radiate to the shoulder; point tenderness over the liver and a right-sided pleural effusion are common, whereas jaundice is rare (p.1799).
Although the colon is the initial site of infection, fewer than one-third of patients with an amebic abscess have active diarrhea at presentation (p.1799).

Strongly age- and sex-dependent: men aged 30-60 are infected at a rate roughly 10-12 times that of women in the same age group; testosterone-modulated NK-T-cell interferon-gamma signaling is implicated experimentally (p.1798).

Young patients tend to present acutely with prominent symptoms of under 10 days' duration, while older patients from endemic areas more often follow a subacute course over months with weight loss and hepatomegaly; only about one-third of those with chronic presentations are febrile (p.1799).
Of travelers who develop an amebic liver abscess after leaving an endemic area, 95% do so within 5 months (p.1799).
Amebic liver abscesses are always preceded by intestinal colonization, which may be entirely asymptomatic (p.1799).
On imaging, more than 80% of patients symptomatic for over 10 days have a single right-lobe abscess, but about 50% of those symptomatic for under 10 days have multiple abscesses (p.1800).

The classic necrotic 'anchovy paste' contents are variable in color and bacteriologically sterile, composed of granular debris with few or no cells; amebae, when present, sit near the abscess capsule rather than in the aspirable necrotic center (p.1799).

Liver enzymes are usually normal or only minimally elevated even with large abscesses; alkaline phosphatase is the most commonly elevated value, while aminotransferase elevation suggests acute disease or a complication (p.1800).
Invasive amebiasis does not elicit eosinophilia (p.1800).
harrison.pathophysiology: Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites invade colonic mucosal venules and travel via the portal venous system to the liver; the organism is resistant to complement-mediated lysis, which is critical to its survival in the bloodstream. An early acute infiltrate (predominantly neutrophils) is followed by lysis of those neutrophils on contact with amebae, and the released neutrophil toxins are thought to contribute to hepatocyte necrosis. The liver parenchyma is progressively replaced by necrotic material surrounded by a thin rim of congested liver tissue, producing the classically described (but variably colored) 'anchovy paste' that is sterile and largely acellular, with amebae found mainly at the capsule. Genetically, a leptin-receptor substitution (Q223R) increases the risk of amebic liver abscess in adults (p.1798-1799).
additionalDifferentials: Pyogenic liver abscess (the most important imaging-based distinction once a hepatic abscess is identified) (p.1801)
Any febrile illness with few localizing signs / fever of unknown origin, since 10-15% present with fever alone (p.1799, p.1801)
nonInfectiousMimics: Pulmonary disease presenting with right-sided pleural/pleuritic findings (p.1801)
additionalInvestigations: Serum alkaline phosphatase and aminotransferases (enzymes often normal/minimally elevated; raised aminotransferases suggest acute disease or complication) (p.1800)
Full blood count for leukocytosis >10,000/uL, present in about three-quarters of patients, especially with acute or complicated disease (p.1800)
Enzyme immunoassay for the Gal/GalNAc lectin antigen, usable on stool and on liver-abscess aspirates (p.1800)
Multiplex PCR for E. histolytica DNA (near 100% sensitivity/specificity) (p.1800)
Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) on abscess pus as a low-cost molecular option (p.1800)
Diagnostic aspirate sent for Gram stain and bacterial culture when distinguishing amebic from pyogenic abscess (p.1801)
redFlags: Pleuropulmonary involvement (reported in 20-30%, the most frequent complication): contiguous spread or frank rupture into the pleural space, the latter requiring drainage (p.1799).
Large abscess (>10 cm) in the superior right lobe, which may rupture into the pleural space (p.1800).
Left-lobe abscess, which may rupture into the pericardium, the complication carrying the gravest prognosis and able to occur even during medical therapy (p.1799-1800).
Rupture into the peritoneum, presenting as an indolent leak or as an acute abdomen (p.1799).
Hepatobronchial fistula causing cough productive of large amounts of necrotic material (p.1799).
Lack of clinical response within 3-5 days or threat of imminent rupture (p.1801).
harrison.prognosis: With early diagnosis and treatment, mortality from uncomplicated amebic liver abscess is under 1%, and over 90% of patients respond dramatically with reduced pain and fever within 72 hours; recurrence is rare. Abscesses resolve slowly and may even enlarge despite clinical improvement, so follow-up ultrasonography can be misleading; complete resolution within 6 months is expected in about two-thirds of patients, while roughly 10% have persistent imaging abnormalities for up to a year. A hepatobronchial fistula carries a good prognosis, whereas pericardial rupture (usually from left-lobe abscesses) carries the gravest prognosis (p.1799-1801).
pitfalls: Expecting concurrent dysentery: fewer than one-third of patients have active diarrhea, so a negative stool examination or absent diarrhea does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1799).
Trophozoites are rarely recovered from liver aspirates because they reside in the abscess capsule, not in the necrotic center that is actually aspirated (p.1799).
Up to 10% of patients with acute amebic liver abscess have negative serology early; titers usually become positive within a week (p.1799).

Microscopy cannot distinguish E. histolytica cysts from non-pathogenic E. dispar, E. moshkovskii, or E. bangladeshi; species-specific diagnosis on microscopy requires seeing trophozoites that have ingested erythrocytes (p.1799).
In endemic areas serology may stay positive for years (indirect hemagglutination up to ~10 years), complicating interpretation (p.1799).
Follow-up imaging may be confusing because abscesses resolve slowly and can transiently enlarge despite a good clinical response (p.1800).
